34. T. rex could become most expensive fossil ever - but it's a ​problem for scientists

**1. Title of the Work**

Who Owns a Bone That Is 67 Million Years Old?

**2. Creative Work**

A fossil is a strange kind of object. It is a rock, but also the remains of a living creature. It is a scientific record, but also something people can admire, display and buy. A dinosaur skeleton can belong to a museum, a university or a private collector. In a deeper sense, it is a piece of Earth's history that no one created.

That raises a difficult question: who should own the fossil record?

The question has become more urgent as dinosaur skeletons sell for astonishing prices. The latest example is a *Tyrannosaurus rex* nicknamed Gus, one of the most complete skeletons of its kind ever found. It was offered at auction by Sotheby's with a pre-sale estimate of $30 million.

**From museum purchase to luxury market**

Dinosaur auctions aren't new. In 1997, Sotheby's sold a *T. rex* named Sue for about $8 million. The buyer was the Field Museum in Chicago, where Sue became a major attraction and an important subject for scientific research.

Much has changed since then. Dinosaur fossils increasingly attract wealthy private buyers as well as museums. The five most expensive dinosaurs ever sold at auction have all been sold since 2020. In 2020, a *T. rex* called Stan sold for $31.8 million, far above its estimate. In 2024, a *Stegosaurus* known as Apex set the auction record at $44.6 million.

For many museums, prices like these are out of reach. Even major institutions say they are increasingly priced out of specimens that could matter for research.

**The work behind a skeleton**

To understand why fossils cost so much, it helps to see what it takes to recover one.

Gus was found in the Badlands of South Dakota, a rugged landscape of eroded hills and exposed rock. The dinosaur was named after Gary "Gus" Licking, the late cattle rancher on whose land it was discovered. The *T. rex* lived about 67 million years ago.

Finding the bones was only the beginning. Excavation can only happen during the warmer field season, when the ground isn't frozen. For three years, the team carefully dug out the skeleton, racing against the return of winter each year. Then they spent another three years in the lab, cleaning, documenting, preserving and reconstructing the bones.

Fossil hunting can be physically demanding and dangerous. Collectors may spend months camping in remote areas, facing extreme weather, wild animals and unstable terrain. Many aren't wealthy. They invest their own time and money with no guarantee of finding anything valuable.

Gus is an impressive specimen. About 61% of its bones have been identified, a high proportion for a *T. rex*. The bones also hint at its life: a large bite mark on the skull, possibly from a fight, and ribs that broke and then healed. Every one of those details can help scientists understand how these animals lived.

**Why scientists worry**

For researchers, the real concern isn't simply cost. It is access.

Science depends on evidence that others can check. If a scientist describes a fossil, other scientists must be able to examine the same specimen later to confirm the observations, challenge the conclusions or compare it with new finds. A fossil isn't just an object to look at once. It is a permanent reference point.

That is why leading scientific journals generally won't publish research on fossils held in private collections. A private owner can sell the specimen, move it, restrict access or lose it. If the fossil disappears from public view, the research based on it can no longer be fully tested. In scientific terms, it is almost as if the evidence no longer exists.

Paleontologists also argue that studying ancient life is more important than ever. Earth's environment is changing rapidly, and many scientists believe we may be entering a mass extinction driven by human activity. Fossils provide real evidence of how life responded to past climate change and environmental crises, information that can help us understand the present and future.

There is a public dimension too. Seeing real dinosaur bones in a museum can inspire curiosity about science and the natural world in a way casts and images often can't.

**A treasure to collect or a record to study?**

Part of the problem is that fossils are increasingly treated like works of art. A famous dinosaur skeleton can become a symbol of status, something to own and display. That shift helps drive prices up.

Some wealthy buyers do share their fossils with the public. The buyer of Apex, hedge fund founder Kenneth Griffin, loaned the *Stegosaurus* to the American Museum of Natural History for four years. Museums have long depended on wealthy donors for gifts and loans of important objects.

Fossils raise a special problem, though. A temporary loan may allow visitors to see a skeleton, but it doesn't guarantee that scientists can study it permanently.

**The case for collectors**

Auction houses and commercial fossil hunters argue that the story isn't so simple. Without collectors, many fossils would never be found or saved at all.

Fossils exposed by erosion don't wait patiently for a museum expedition. On England's Jurassic Coast, for example, waves and weather constantly break apart cliffs and rocks. A fossil uncovered one day can be destroyed by the sea the next. Professional collectors who recover these specimens may save them from being lost forever.

Supporters of the commercial trade also argue that prices reflect the skill, effort, expense and risk involved in excavation. If collectors can't earn a living, fewer people may search for fossils at all.

**No place is perfectly safe**

Even museums can't guarantee a fossil will survive forever. In 1829, the famous fossil collector Mary Anning discovered a fossil fish later named *Squaloraja*, an animal related to sharks and rays. It was donated to a museum institution in Bristol, but more than a century later it was destroyed during a bombing raid in the Second World War.

Still, scientists argue that public institutions offer the best long-term chance of keeping fossils accessible, protected and available for future research.

**Beyond the famous giants**

The debate over expensive dinosaurs can hide another truth: most important fossils aren't spectacular skeletons. Many are small, ordinary-looking or overlooked. Some may be scientifically more valuable than a famous *T. rex*, even if they would never attract billionaire buyers.

Small fossils also play a role in public education. Ammonites sold to children at a beach, for example, can spark a lifelong interest in science.

**A shared history**

Collectors, museums and scientists may disagree about who should own fossils, but they share one goal: saving the record of ancient life before it is lost.

The challenge is to balance fair rewards for the people who find fossils with the need to keep important specimens available for science and the public. A dinosaur that survived 67 million years underground is more than a valuable object. It is evidence about Earth's past, and its value depends on people being able to study it for generations.

Some of that primordial heat remains within the planet today.

Another major source comes from radioactive decay.

Earth's average surface heat flow is modest when measured per square meter. Nevertheless, the accumulated heat escaping across the entire planet represents a substantial amount of thermal power.

The challenge for energy production is that heat is not distributed equally in terms of accessibility.

### The Geothermal Gradient

The geothermal gradient describes how temperature changes with depth beneath Earth's surface.

\\[ G=\frac{\Delta T}{\Delta z}, \\]

In many regions of continental crust, temperatures increase by roughly 20–35°C per kilometer, although local values vary substantially.

An illustrative gradient of 30°C per kilometer would produce an increase of approximately 150°C over five kilometers.

However, this does not mean that every location reaches the same temperature at the same depth.

This variation explains why traditional geothermal power plants are concentrated in particular regions.

### How Conventional Geothermal Electricity Works

### The Difference Between Heat and Electricity

A geothermal reservoir contains thermal energy, but that energy cannot be converted completely into electricity.

Thermodynamics imposes fundamental limits.

For an ideal heat engine operating between a hot reservoir at temperature \\(T_h\\) and a cold reservoir at temperature \\(T_c\\), the maximum theoretical efficiency is given by the Carnot relationship:

\\[ \eta\_{\max}=1-\frac{T_c}{T_h}. \\]

Both temperatures must be measured in kelvin.

For example, consider a hypothetical geothermal system operating between a hot reservoir at 200°C and a cooling environment at 20°C.

The corresponding temperatures are approximately 473 K and 293 K.

The ideal maximum efficiency is

\\[ \eta\_{\max}=1-\frac{293}{473}\approx 0.38. \\]

This means that even an idealized system could convert only about 38% of the heat into useful work under those temperature conditions.

Real power plants achieve lower efficiencies because of mechanical, thermal, and other losses.

This relationship explains why higher geothermal temperatures are attractive.

### Levelized Cost of Electricity

A common metric for comparing electricity generation technologies is the levelized cost of electricity, or LCOE.

In simplified terms, it represents the discounted cost of building and operating a power plant divided by its discounted lifetime electricity output.

A general expression is

\\[ \mathrm{LCOE} = \frac{ \displaystyle\sum\_{t=0}^{n} \frac{I_t+M_t+F_t}{(1+r)^t} }{ \displaystyle\sum\_{t=0}^{n} \frac{E_t}{(1+r)^t} }, \\]

where \\(I_t\\) represents investment costs, \\(M_t\\) operation and maintenance costs, \\(F_t\\) fuel costs, \\(E_t\\) electricity generation, and \\(r\\) the discount rate.

For geothermal plants, fuel purchase costs are often negligible.

However, investment and maintenance costs can be significant.

LCOE also does not capture every aspect of electricity-system value.

35. The abundant but expensive energy source that's under your feet

**1. Title of the Work**

The Heat We Walk On

**2. Creative Work**

Every day, people walk across one of the largest energy sources on the planet without noticing it. It doesn't blow like wind or shine like sunlight. It isn't pumped from oil fields or carried in coal trains. It is simply there, beneath roads, farms, forests and cities: the heat inside Earth.

Dig deep enough almost anywhere, and the ground gets hotter. Some of that heat is left over from the planet's formation, and some comes from the slow decay of radioactive elements in rock. It has been there for billions of years and will last far longer than human civilization. The challenge has never been whether this energy exists. It has been how to reach it affordably.

**Why geothermal has stayed in the background**

Geothermal energy uses underground heat to produce electricity or warm buildings. In conventional systems, wells reach underground reservoirs of hot water or steam. The steam drives turbines to generate electricity, and the cooled water can then be returned underground.

The approach works especially well in places where hot rock and water sit close to the surface, often in volcanic areas or near the boundaries of tectonic plates. Iceland, for example, uses geothermal energy extensively for electricity and heating.

Most of the world isn't so lucky. In many regions, usable heat lies deep underground, inside hard rock, without enough natural water flowing through it. Reaching it is technically difficult and expensive. So geothermal has supplied only a small share of global energy, even though the resource itself is enormous.

**Drilling into a new generation**

A new wave of technology aims to change that.

One approach is called enhanced geothermal systems, or EGS. Instead of relying on natural underground reservoirs, engineers create their own. They drill into hot rock and pump in pressurized fluid to open small fractures. Water can then be injected through one well, flow through the heated cracks and come up hot through another well, where its energy can be used.

The method uses techniques similar to hydraulic fracturing, or fracking, which became controversial in the oil and gas industry. The purpose is very different. Instead of extracting fossil fuels, EGS aims to harvest heat for low-emission electricity. Like any technology that changes underground rock, it carries risks, including possible small earthquakes, and projects need careful monitoring. Supporters argue that the climate benefits of a constant, renewable power source make those risks worth managing.

**Melting through rock**

Reaching deeper, hotter rock may require entirely new ways of drilling.

Conventional drill bits wear out quickly in extremely hard rock at high temperatures. Replacing them costs time and money. Some companies are developing tougher drilling systems. Others are trying to avoid traditional drill bits altogether.

Quaise, a company with roots at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, is developing millimeter-wave drilling. The technique uses powerful electromagnetic waves, related to the microwaves used in household ovens, to melt and vaporize rock. Without a physical bit grinding through stone, there is nothing to wear down.

The goal is to reach "superhot" rock at temperatures between about 300 and 500 degrees Celsius. Hotter rock can deliver much more energy from each well, potentially around ten times more than lower-temperature systems. That could make geothermal energy far more economical and allow it to be produced in many places, not just geological hotspots.

Quaise is developing a project in Oregon, with the aim of having it running by 2030. The company says its system will need a large amount of water at first, but that water can then circulate repeatedly through the hot rock instead of being constantly replaced.

Other companies are exploring different drilling ideas, including projectiles fired at very high speeds to break through rock.

**The price of getting started**

The biggest barrier is still cost.

Next-generation geothermal plants require huge upfront investment in drilling, equipment and testing. Early projects also face uncertainty. They may run into technical problems or cost more than expected. One reason geothermal is expensive today is that a well drilled for heat generally produces less energy value than a well drilled for oil or gas.

Fervo Energy, a Texas-based company, gives one example of both the promise and the challenge. In May, it became the first next-generation geothermal company to be publicly traded, with an initial valuation of about $7.7 billion. Fervo reports that building its plant in Utah costs about $7,000 per kilowatt of electricity capacity, comparable to traditional nuclear power.

That is expensive, but geothermal plants have an important advantage once running: they need no fuel. There are no ongoing costs for coal, gas or uranium. Fervo hopes that as the industry grows and techniques improve, costs will fall enough for geothermal to compete with natural gas.

Large technology companies are interested because data centers need huge amounts of reliable electricity. Fervo has agreed to supply energy to Google and has support from Breakthrough Energy, an investment group founded by Bill Gates. Still, the International Energy Agency has noted that demand from data centers alone won't be enough to make geothermal a major global energy source. Much broader investment will be needed.

**Energy that doesn't depend on the weather**

Geothermal energy has a feature many other renewable sources lack: it can run almost all the time. Solar power depends on daylight and wind power on weather, so both need storage or backup to supply electricity around the clock. Geothermal plants can generate steadily, day and night, through every season.

That makes geothermal a potentially valuable partner for other clean energy sources. It could help stabilize electricity grids as societies move away from fossil fuels.

Geothermal also appeals to people with different priorities. Some value it mainly for its low greenhouse gas emissions. Others see it as a way to increase energy independence and to use the drilling skills and equipment already developed by the oil and gas industry. In the United States, that broad appeal has helped geothermal win support across political lines, including proposed legislation to support research and development of next-generation systems.

Supporters also point out that fuels such as oil and gas are traded globally and vulnerable to political disruption. Geothermal heat is local. Once the technology exists, the energy source sits beneath a country's own land.

**A resource waiting for the right tools**

History shows that energy technologies can become much cheaper as they mature. Over the past few decades, solar panels went from expensive niche products to one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many parts of the world. Advocates hope geothermal can follow a similar path as drilling improves and projects scale up.

Success isn't guaranteed. The technology must prove reliable, safe and affordable. Early projects have to show they can deliver on their promises without serious environmental problems or uncontrolled costs.

The opportunity is still huge. Beneath almost every community lies a source of clean, constant energy that has been warming the planet for billions of years. The question isn't whether the heat is there. It is whether engineers can reach it reliably and cheaply enough to make it a major part of our energy supply.

36. The AI Revolution in Math Has Arrived

**1. Title of the Work**

A New Apprentice in the Workshop

**2. Creative Work**

Imagine an old workshop where skilled craftspeople have spent their lives learning a difficult trade. One day a new apprentice arrives. It never gets tired. It can try a thousand designs overnight, has read nearly every manual ever written and sometimes produces ideas so clever that the masters stop and stare. It also makes bizarre mistakes that no beginner would make, and it doesn't always know when it is wrong.

How should the workshop respond? Should it welcome the apprentice, fear it, or carefully change how the work is done?

That is roughly the situation mathematics now faces. In a remarkably short time, artificial intelligence has gone from a curiosity to a working tool in mathematical research, and mathematicians are trying to understand what that means for their discipline.

**The moment people started paying attention**

For years, many mathematicians doubted that AI could do serious mathematics. Language models often produced convincing-sounding but incorrect arguments. They seemed better at imitating mathematical writing than at reasoning reliably.

That view began to change in July 2025, when several AI systems solved five of the six problems at the International Mathematical Olympiad, one of the world's hardest competitions for young mathematicians. Olympiad problems aren't research problems, since they already have known solutions. Still, the results surprised many experts and led some skeptical researchers to try AI for themselves.

What they found went beyond solving puzzles. AI systems began helping mathematicians search the literature, test ideas, find examples and even discover proofs. By early 2026, a challenge called First Proof tested AI systems on ten research-level questions chosen to be unlikely to appear in their training data. The systems, with varying amounts of human guidance, solved more than half of them.

**Doing many experiments at once**

One of the clearest changes is scale.

Traditionally, a mathematician might spend months or years on one problem. AI makes it possible to explore many problems at once. Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve system shows how. It uses a language model to write computer programs that search for mathematical constructions, then improves those programs through an evolutionary process, keeping promising versions and modifying them again and again.

Mathematicians including Terence Tao and Javier Gómez-Serrano worked with DeepMind researchers to try AlphaEvolve on 67 problems across different areas of mathematics. In 23 cases, it slightly improved the best known results. In 36 others, it matched existing results. None of these advances was a world-changing breakthrough, but together they showed something new. Results that might have taken a specialist months could sometimes be reached in a day or two, even by researchers who weren't experts in that particular field.

Supporters describe this as finding "low-hanging fruit" more efficiently: searching large sets of problems for cases where progress is possible. The successes still sit among many failures that never appear in published papers.

**A partner for thinking**

AI has also become a kind of mathematical conversation partner.

Researchers increasingly discuss problems with language models in long back-and-forth exchanges. The models often make errors, sometimes very basic ones. Yet within those flawed answers, they can also suggest useful directions, partial results or new connections. Some mathematicians find the experience frustrating. Others treat it like brainstorming with an unusual collaborator: discard the bad ideas, keep the good ones and check everything carefully.

Ernest Ryu, then at the University of California, Los Angeles, used this approach on a question about an optimization method proposed by Yurii Nesterov in 1983. Optimization methods help computers find the lowest point of a mathematical "landscape," a task central to training modern machine-learning systems. Nesterov's method moves faster by using information from earlier steps, but no one had proved that it always settles at the correct minimum instead of overshooting forever.

When Ryu worked on the problem with ChatGPT, the model repeatedly gave flawed proofs. Some of the steps leading up to its mistakes were correct and useful. Ryu checked the output, kept the valid parts and fed them back into new prompts. Within days, he found a proof. He described his role as the verifier, the person who made sure the reasoning really worked.

**Discovering what no one asked for**

Sometimes AI finds things researchers weren't even looking for.

A group of mathematicians studying permutation groups, the mathematical structures that describe ways of shuffling a set of objects, wanted to find especially complex relationships between different shuffles. They used AlphaEvolve to search for examples. The program produced code that revealed an unexpected pattern. In certain cases, especially when the number of objects was a power of two, the relationships formed higher-dimensional cubes called hypercubes.

The structure had been present in the mathematics for decades, but no one had noticed it. The AI hadn't been asked to find hypercubes. It found them while working toward a different goal, and human mathematicians then recognized their significance.

In another project, mathematician Ravi Vakil and colleagues used Google's AI tools to prove a simpler version of a problem about embedding spheres into complex geometric spaces. The AI's proof was clear and elegant, and it showed the researchers a structure that helped them understand the more general case. Afterward, they faced an unusual question: who deserved credit for the key idea, the humans or the machine?

**The problem of trust**

As AI produces more mathematics, verification becomes crucial. A proof is only valuable if it is correct. Mathematicians are already worried about a flood of low-quality, AI-generated papers sent to journals, adding to the burden on reviewers.

One promising answer is formal verification. Proofs are translated into precise computer languages, and software checks that each logical step follows correctly. Formalizing proofs has traditionally been slow and demanding, but AI may help automate the process. If that works, mathematicians could use AI to generate ideas while relying on independent verification systems to confirm the results.

**What happens to learning?**

The biggest concern may be education. Mathematical skill is built through struggle: working through exercises, making mistakes and slowly developing intuition. If AI can solve many homework problems instantly, students may lose chances to build that understanding.

Some professors have already reduced take-home assignments because they can't tell whether students did the work themselves. Researchers worry that AI could speed up the work of experienced mathematicians while making it harder to train the next generation.

Access is another issue. Some advanced AI systems are available only to researchers working with large technology companies. Without fair access, the new tools could widen existing gaps between institutions and countries.

**More than a science**

Even enthusiastic supporters don't expect AI to replace mathematicians completely, at least for now. Current AI systems are good at short, impressive leaps. They can solve some difficult pieces of a problem or spot overlooked patterns. Humans are still better at choosing important questions, planning long research programs and building deep theories over many years.

Nobody knows how long that will remain true. Progress has been rapid, and some mathematicians expect AI to eventually outperform humans in many measurable aspects of research.

Mathematics isn't only about producing correct statements. It is also about understanding, explanation and taste. There are endless ways to describe the same mathematical truth, and mathematicians choose among them based on clarity, elegance and meaning. In that sense, mathematics resembles an art as well as a science. Some researchers worry that if the field focuses only on producing more results faster, it could lose part of what makes it valuable.

**Changing the workshop**

The arrival of AI doesn't have to end the mathematical craft, but it will change it. The masters in the workshop may spend less time on routine searches and more on asking good questions, judging which results matter and making sure the work is correct. Teachers may need new ways to help students develop understanding. The community will need new rules for credit, access and verification.

The new apprentice is powerful, fast and sometimes brilliant. It is also unpredictable and needs careful supervision. How mathematics uses it will depend not only on what the technology can do, but on what mathematicians decide is worth keeping in their craft.

For millennia, the pursuit of mathematics has been a profoundly human craft—a slow, meticulous ascent up jagged peaks of logic. ### When Competition Stops Producing Competitive Prices

Imagine a city where two companies sell nearly identical products.

### Why Prices Matter in Competitive Markets

Prices perform several important economic functions.

They communicate information about scarcity, demand, and production costs.

They influence which products consumers purchase.

They also determine the revenue businesses receive.

In a competitive market, a company must consider what rival firms are charging.

If products are nearly identical, customers have little reason to purchase the more expensive option unless other factors matter.

For example, consider two companies producing an identical item at a marginal cost of $10.

If one charges $25 and the other charges $20, many customers may prefer the cheaper seller.

The first company can respond by reducing its price.

The process may continue until prices approach production costs, subject to the assumptions of the market model.

In economics, this situation resembles Bertrand competition.

The classical model illustrates how price competition between even a small number of sellers can create strong pressure toward lower prices.

However, the conclusion depends on assumptions.

Products must be sufficiently similar.

Customers must be able to compare prices.

Firms must possess adequate capacity.

And each seller must respond to the incentives created by its competitors.

When pricing decisions are delegated to learning algorithms, these interactions can become more complicated.

### The Traditional Problem of Collusion

Collusion occurs when competing businesses coordinate their behavior to reduce competition.

A familiar example is price fixing.

Two sellers might agree not to lower prices below a particular level.

Instead of competing aggressively, they protect each other's profit margins.

Consumers may then pay more than they would under ordinary competition.

Competition laws in many jurisdictions prohibit certain agreements among competitors because they undermine market rivalry.

Traditional enforcement often seeks evidence of coordination.

Regulators may examine communications, meetings, documents, or other indications that businesses agreed to restrict competition.

This approach reflects the historical image of collusion.

Representatives of different companies meet privately and establish a plan.

But algorithmic markets introduce a complication.

A computer program can respond to another program's behavior without communicating an explicit agreement.

Modern businesses collect enormous amounts of information about markets.

They can observe competitors' prices.

They may analyze inventory levels, time of day, seasonal patterns, and purchasing behavior.

More sophisticated approaches may learn from repeated interactions.

The program changes a price, observes the resulting profit, and updates its strategy.

A learning algorithm does not need to understand the moral or legal significance of its actions.

\\[ \pi(p)=\bigl(p-c\bigr)D(p), \\]

where \\(p\\) is the selling price, \\(c\\) is marginal production cost, and \\(D(p)\\) is demand at that price.

In a market with competing sellers, demand also depends on rival prices.

For firm \\(i\\), profit might therefore be represented as

\\[ \pi_i(p_i,p_j) = (p_i-c_i)D_i(p_i,p_j). \\]

### The Game-Theoretic View of Pricing

Game theory studies situations in which the outcomes of decisions depend on the choices of multiple participants.

A business chooses a price.

In a simplified two-player game, the payoffs can be written as

\\[ u_1(a_1,a_2) \quad\text{and}\quad u_2(a_1,a_2), \\]

where \\(a_1\\) and \\(a_2\\) represent the actions of the two players.

In a pricing game, the actions are prices.

The payoffs are profits.

Game theory allows researchers to investigate whether strategies will remain stable, whether cooperation is possible, and whether individually rational behavior can produce undesirable collective outcomes.

This mathematical framework becomes especially useful when algorithms repeatedly compete against one another.

### The Prisoner's Dilemma and the Logic of Cooperation

One of the most famous examples in game theory is the prisoner's dilemma.

Two players can cooperate or defect.

Mutual cooperation produces a better collective outcome than mutual defection.

Yet each player may possess an individual incentive to defect.

The resulting equilibrium can therefore be worse for both players than cooperation would have been.

But each may be tempted to undercut the other and capture more customers.

### The Discovery of Tacit Algorithmic Collusion

An influential 2019 study examined learning algorithms competing in a simulated pricing market.

The researchers allowed the algorithms to adjust their strategies through repeated interaction.

Neither algorithm received an explicit instruction to collude.

Nevertheless, the systems learned behavior that supported elevated prices.

When one algorithm reduced its price, the other could respond with an aggressive price reduction.

However, it emerged through learning rather than an explicit agreement.
